lesson.title: Triads
lesson.summary: Three notes stacked in thirds make a triad: major, minor, diminished or augmented, in root position or inverted.

section.title: Stacking thirds
section.p: A triad is a chord of three notes stacked in thirds. The bottom note of the stack is the root, which names the triad. The note a third above the root is the third, and the note a fifth above the root is the fifth.

figure.caption: A triad on C: the root C, the third E and the fifth G.

section.p: Written as a compact stack with the root at the bottom, a triad sits on three neighbouring lines or in three neighbouring spaces, so it is easy to recognise on the staff.

check.prompt: Which note is the fifth of the triad F–A–C?
check.explanation: The root is F, the third is A, a third above it, and the fifth is C, a fifth above the root.

section.title: The four qualities
section.p: The quality of a triad depends on the size of its two thirds:

list.li: Major: a major third with a minor third above it. The fifth from the root is perfect.
Minor: a minor third with a major third above it. The fifth from the root is perfect.
Diminished: two minor thirds. The fifth from the root is diminished.
Augmented: two major thirds. The fifth from the root is augmented.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4]/h | [C4 Eb4 G4]/h | [C4 Eb4 Gb4]/h | [C4 E4 G#4]/h
figure.caption: Major, minor, diminished and augmented triads on C.

section.p: Major triads sound bright and minor triads darker. Diminished triads sound tense and augmented triads unsettled; both are much rarer than major and minor.

worked.title: Identify the quality of a triad

step.p: Take D–F–A. Name the lower third: D major has F#, so D–F is a minor third.
Name the upper third: F major has A, so F–A is a major third.
A minor third below a major third makes a minor triad. As a check, the fifth D–A is perfect. The triad is D minor.

check.prompt: Which of these triads is diminished?
check.explanation: B–D and D–F are both minor thirds, and the fifth B–F is diminished. B–D–F# is minor and B–D#–F# is major.

check.prompt: What is the quality of this triad?

figure.description: A triad on the bottom three lines of the treble staff, with a sharp before the middle note.

check.explanation: The notes are E, G# and B. E–G# is a major third and G#–B a minor third, so the triad is major. Without the sharp, E–G–B would be minor.

section.title: Inversions
section.p: The lowest note of a chord, the bass, need not be the root. Which chord member is in the bass decides the position of the triad:

list.li: Root position: the root is in the bass.
First inversion: the third is in the bass.
Second inversion: the fifth is in the bass.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4]/h [E4 G4 C5]/h [G4 C5 E5]/h
figure.caption: A C major triad in root position, first inversion and second inversion.

section.p: Only the bass matters. The upper notes can be in any order and spread out, and notes can be doubled; the chord is still the same triad in the same position.

figure.caption: With E in the bass, this spread C major triad is in first inversion.

section.p: Inversions are also named after the intervals above the bass, as in figured bass: a first-inversion triad is a six-three chord (6/3, usually shortened to 6, a six chord), and a second-inversion triad a six-four chord (6/4).

worked.title: Find the root of an inverted triad

step.p: Take the notes E, G and C, from the bottom up. They are not stacked in thirds: G–C is a fourth.
Rearrange the notes until they stack in thirds, on neighbouring lines or spaces: C–E–G. The bottom note of the stack, C, is the root.
Compare with the bass. The bass was E, the third, so the chord is a C major triad in first inversion.

check.prompt: In a first-inversion triad, which chord member is the lowest note?
check.explanation: First inversion puts the third in the bass; second inversion puts the fifth there, and root position the root.

check.prompt: Name the root, quality and position of this triad.

figure.description: Three notes sounding together in the treble clef: the lowest in the second space, the others on the fourth line and on the top line.

check.explanation: The notes A, D and F stack in thirds as D–F–A: a minor third and a major third, so D minor. The bass, A, is the fifth, so the triad is in second inversion.

section.title: Triads in a key
section.p: A triad can be built on every degree of a scale, using only the notes of the key. Roman numerals name these triads by the degree of their root. Upper case means major, lower case minor; a small circle (°) means diminished and a plus sign (+) augmented.

figure.staff: [C4 E4 G4]/h{I} [D4 F4 A4]/h{ii} [E4 G4 B4]/h{iii} [F4 A4 C5]/h{IV} [G4 B4 D5]/h{V} [A4 C5 E5]/h{vi} [B4 D5 F5]/h{vii°}
figure.caption: The triads of C major.

section.p: Every major key has the same pattern: I, IV and V are major; ii, iii and vi are minor; vii° is diminished. The three major triads, on the tonic, subdominant and dominant, are the primary triads of the key.

In minor keys the seventh degree varies, and so do the triads that contain it. The usual triads in minor take the raised seventh, the leading tone, for V and vii°, and the lowered seventh for III: i, ii°, III, iv, V, VI and vii°. The leading tone makes V a major triad, which pulls more strongly to the tonic.

figure.staff: [A2 C3 E3]/h{i} [B2 D3 F3]/h{ii°} [C3 E3 G3]/h{III} [D3 F3 A3]/h{iv} [E3 G#3 B3]/h{V} [F3 A3 C4]/h{VI} [G#3 B3 D4]/h{vii°}
figure.caption: The usual triads of A minor. V and vii° contain the leading tone G#.

section.p: The lowered seventh of natural minor gives a minor v and a major VII instead. Both occur in common-practice music, but less often and mostly in particular contexts: VII, for example, often leads to III. With the raised seventh, III becomes augmented, III+, which is rare.

check.prompt: In G major, what is the quality of the triad on the sixth degree?
check.explanation: The sixth degree of G major is E, and the triad E–G–B is minor: vi in every major key.

check.prompt: Which notes form the V triad in D major?
check.explanation: The fifth degree of D major is A. The key has C#, so the triad is A–C#–E, a major triad. G–B–D is IV.

check.prompt: In a minor key, what is the quality of V when it uses the leading tone?
check.explanation: In A minor, V is E–G#–B: a major third and a minor third, so a major triad. With the subtonic G it would be the minor v.
